title: Egress and Survival Branch
description: The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center's Egress and Survival branch acquires and supports United States Air Force aircrew life support equipment, like ejection seats and parachutes, to ensure they function correctly when our warfighters need it, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, Aug. 14, 2018. AFLCMC is one of six centers under Air Force Materiel Command and is the single center responsible for total life cycle management of Air Force weapon systems. (U.S. Air Force video by Ryan Law)
keywords: Ejection Seat, Wright-Patt, life sciences lab, AIr Force, engineer, parachute

transcript.text: - [Narrator] In an airman's moment of greatest need,
the Eggress and Survival Branch provides the equipment
that could be the difference between life and death.
- I love to come to work every day
because I know when I do my job right,
that airmen get to come home to their families.
From the worst situation that they can imagine,
we give them what they need to get out of there.
- [Narrator] One critical component
of the Eggress and Survival Branch
is the Life Sciences Equipment Laboratory.
- This lab was established back
at Kelly Air Force Base in 1965.
The mission that carries here is to keep the quality
of the Air Force life support equipment at a higher level.
- When an emergency occurs aboard
United States Air Force aircraft
and aircrew flight equipment
or Eggress products are involved,
then the Life Sciences Equipment Lab
tries to determine if the products
function successfully or if they didn't.
And if they didn't function successfully,
then we'll determine why that was
and make recommendations to make sure
that those products function in the future.
Mishap investigations are our best opportunity
to assess the performance of our products
because you don't get a test that's more realistic,
more real to life, than an actual crash environment.
- [Narrator] The Life Sciences Equipment Laboratory
has investigated over 420 mishap cases to date.
- Many items come through the lab.
We are in charge of conducting testing
on the Air Force life support equipment,
so there's variety of equipment that comes in,
such as parachutes,
ejection seat parts, harnesses, you name it.
- [Narrator] One important project the branch is working on
is the transition from the outdated legacy parachute system
to a new low-profile parachute system.
- The driving force is more of a modernization effort
to reduce burden on the aircrew members
as well as maintainers.
Roughly, the legacy one is more like,
probably, about four hours for an experienced individual,
inspecting all the components and doing the repacks
and things of that nature.
The newer system,
because of its modernization simplicity,
it takes anywhere from an hour to two at tops.
- [Narrator] The laboratory also has
a special project mission.
- In Materials and Textiles Lab
within the Eggress and Survival Branch
provides the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center
with first-order
rapid testing
of textiles and hardware.
- [Narrator] This allows the lab to provide timely testing
at a fraction of the cost.
- A tensile test equipment
is important for things like chutes
because when you come out of a aircraft,
you're traveling at several hundred miles an hour,
so that chute has to slow you down
and the force of all the equipment
and a seat coming out of the aircraft
and the chute going behind it is significant enough
that it could shred the chutes.
We come in and actually put that load on the equipment
and make sure that it's not gonna fail another load.
- We believe
the lab has a very critical mission
to the Air Force because we stop
bad parts from going into the Air Force.
Bad parts cost money
and if impact the mission
and, at the end, could cost life.
So, we feel that we save lives,
we improve the mission,
and we save money for the Air Force.
